22. Chapter on Praising the Buddha (Buddhastava-varga), the twenty-second chapter of the *Dhammapada*. This chapter, consisting of twenty-one sections, extols the divine virtues of the Buddha; nothing he does fails to benefit and deliver others, clearly establishing him as a model for the world.
Having triumphed oneself, one does not receive evil; having triumphed over all the world, one’s sagely wisdom is vast and boundless.
Opening the eyes of the ignorant, one leads them into the Way.
Having severed the net of afflictions, there is no obstruction; with craving exhausted, nothing remains to be accumulated.
The Buddha’s intent is profound and boundless; he causes those who have not yet trodden the path to tread it.
Valiantly establishing a single mind, he leaves the household life and extinguishes [defilements] day and night.
With the roots severed and no desire in his heart, he trains in right mindfulness and clarity.

Pure through the vision of the truths, free from defilement, and having already crossed the abyss of the five realms of existence, the Buddha has appeared to illuminate the world and eliminate the manifold sorrows and sufferings of beings.
Difficult is it to obtain birth in the human realm; difficult is it to obtain a long life.
In this world, it is rare for a Buddha to appear; the Buddha’s Dharma is difficult to hear.
Since I have no refuge or protection, and am likewise without a companion, I shall accumulate the practice of a single path to attain Buddhahood, spontaneously penetrating the Holy Way.
The boatman can cross the waters; diligence serves as the bridge.
Those bound by lineage are mere men; those who cross over are the heroic ones.
One who destroys evil and crosses over is a Buddha; one who rests upon the ground is a brahmin.
The *bhikṣu* studies the Dharma; the disciple severs the seeds [of rebirth].
Contemplative practice and patience are foremost; the Buddha says Nirvāṇa is supreme.
Having abandoned transgression to become a śramaṇa, one does no harm to others.
Neither harassing nor causing distress, upholding all precepts as they are;
eating little and abandoning attachment to the body, dwelling in secluded places;
with a mind that is attentive and discerning—one is able to honor the Buddha’s teaching.
Commit no evil; Practice all that is good; Purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The Buddha is the Honored One, Who has severed the outflows and is free from lust; The Hero among the Śākyas, Whose entire retinue follows his heart.
How joyful is the retribution of merit! All that is wished for is accomplished; one is swift in attaining supreme tranquility and personally reaches Nirvāṇa.
Yet many take refuge in mountains, rivers, and tree spirits, or establish temples with images, offering sacrifices to seek blessings.
Taking refuge in such [a way] is neither auspicious nor supreme; they cannot come to deliver me from my manifold sufferings.
But if one takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha, and in the Path, the Virtue, and the Four Truths, one will surely perceive right wisdom.
Birth and death are extreme suffering; one attains deliverance through the Truths. The Eightfold Path transcends the world;
by this, all sufferings are eliminated.
Taking refuge in the Triple Gem—the most auspicious, the supreme, and the only such refuge—one crosses over all suffering.
A person who is upright and impartial, whose will is set on the Way and who is not stingy—how beneficial such a person is!
One who has taken refuge in the Buddha is difficult to encounter;
they are truly peerless, and wherever they are born, [they bring light].
May our kinsmen receive blessings;
may the arising of all Buddhas be a joy, and the preaching of the sutras and the Way be a joy. May the assembly be harmonious and joyful; through harmony, there is constant peace.

Chapter 23: On Tranquility (Khantivāda). This chapter of the Dhammapada, consisting of fourteen sections, ranks the secure against the perilous; it teaches that by abandoning evil and embracing the good, one attains joy without falling away.
My life is already at peace; I do not resent those who harbor resentment toward me. While others harbor resentment, I act without resentment.
My life is already at peace; I am not afflicted by the afflictions of others. While others are afflicted, I act without affliction.
My life is already secure; I am not distressed by sorrow. While people everywhere possess sorrow, my conduct is free from sorrow.
My life is already secure, pure and unconditioned; I take joy as my sustenance, like the devas of Ābhāsvara.
My life is already at peace; tranquil and free from affairs, even if the fires of the world burn with abundant fuel, how could they ever consume me?
Victory gives rise to resentment, while defeat leads to self-contempt; by casting off the mind of victory and defeat, one is naturally at peace without contention.
There is no heat greater than lust; there is no poison greater than anger; there is no suffering greater than the body;
there is no bliss greater than cessation.
Without pleasure, with little pleasure, with little eloquence, and with little wisdom—those who contemplate and seek the Great shall attain Great Peace.
I am the World-Honored One; long liberated and free from sorrow, I have rightly crossed over the three realms of existence and alone subdued the hosts of Māra.
It is a joy to behold the Noble Ones; it is a joy to find refuge in them; it is a joy to be separated from fools.
It is a joy to be virtuous and solitary; it is a joy to uphold the Right Path; it is a joy to be skillful in preaching the Dharma.
One who does not contend with the world;

whose observance of precepts is constant and joyful, and who dwells in joy by relying on the virtuous; who gathers like kinsmen meeting, drawing near to the benevolent and wise, and who is deeply learned and far-reaching.
Life is short and the passing away from the world is many; one who studies should grasp the essentials so as to reach peace in old age.
Those who wish to attain the nectar [of immortality] find joy in abandoning desire and realizing the truth of cessation.
Desiring to cross over the suffering of birth and death, one should partake of the flavor of the ambrosia.

Chapter 24: Delight (*Nandana-varga*) The Chapter on Delight, the twenty-fourth of the *Dharmapada*, consists of twelve sections. Regarding this chapter: it restrains excessive delight; if one can be free from craving and desire, then there will be no sorrow or affliction.
To oppose the Way is to follow one's own whims; to follow the Way is to oppose one's whims.
To abandon righteousness for what one desires is to follow the dictates of craving.
One should not pursue what is loved, nor should one harbor what is disliked.
One grieves when not seeing those one loves; one also grieves when seeing those one does not love.
Therefore, do not create attachment, for attachment is the source from which hatred arises.
For one who has already eliminated the fetters, there is neither love nor anything to hate.
From attachment and delight arises sorrow; from attachment and delight arises fear.
Without attachment and delight, what is there to sorrow over?
What is there to fear?
Attachment to pleasure gives rise to sorrow; attachment to pleasure gives rise to fear.
Having nothing to which one is attached, what is there to sorrow?
What is there to fear?
Craving gives rise to sorrow; craving gives rise to fear.
When one is free from craving, what is there to sorrow over?
What is there to fear?
When one is free from greed, the precepts are perfected; with utmost sincerity and a sense of shame, one’s conduct brings one close to the Path, and one becomes beloved by the multitude.
When lustful tendencies do not emerge, one speaks only after reflecting on what is right; with no craving in the heart, one will surely cut off the stream and cross over.
Just as a person who has traveled for a long time returns safely from afar, bringing peace to his kin and loved ones, and they rejoice at his arrival;
so too does one who delights in practicing merit go from this world to the next, personally receiving blessings and rejoicing like those welcoming a returning kinsman.
Arising from the noble teachings, one restrains what is unwholesome; draw near to those who see and love the Path, and distance yourself from those who leave the Path—do not befriend them.
Whether one draws near or does not draw near, the state in which they dwell differs: by drawing near to the Path one ascends to heaven; by not drawing near, one falls into hell.

Chapter 25: On Anger. The twenty-sixth chapter of the Dhammapada, "On Anger," shows that one who perceives the harm of hatred and remains broad-minded, compassionate, and gentle is protected by the heavens and loved by men.
In anger one does not see the Dharma; in anger one does not know the Path.
He who can eliminate anger—happiness and merit will always follow him.
In lust one does not see the Dharma; the same is true for the mind of delusion.
He who abandons lust and removes delusion possesses the most supreme merit.
One who can restrain anger as one stops a runaway chariot is a skilled driver;
he casts off darkness and enters into light.
Patience triumphs over anger; goodness triumphs over evil. The victor is able to give; sincerity triumphs over deception.
One who does not deceive, does not become angry, and does not harbor many desires—by these three qualities, one ascends to heaven after death.
Always restraining the body, with a compassionate heart refraining from killing, one will be born in heaven and reach that state where there is no sorrow.
With a mind always alert and awake, clearly aspiring to diligent study, and with outflows exhausted and the mind liberated, one may attain Nirvāṇa.
From antiquity to the present, some have disparaged the talkative, others have disparaged the silent and patient, and yet others have disparaged the moderate;
there is nothing in the world that has not been disparaged. When one’s desires are not noble, one cannot maintain moderation.
One disparages and one praises, yet it is all for the sake of profit and fame; those praised by the wise are alone called "virtuous.
When a person of wisdom observes the precepts, they are beyond reproach or slander; like the purity of an Arhat, do not falsely accuse them.
Praised by all people and extolled by Brahmā and Śakra, one should always guard the body with vigilance to restrain anger;

by eliminating bodily misconduct, one advances in the cultivation of virtuous conduct. One should always guard speech with vigilance to restrain anger; [by eliminating verbal misconduct, one advances in the cultivation of virtuous conduct].
Eliminate evil speech from the mouth and recite the words of the Dharma; always maintain a cautious mind to guard against anger.
Remove evil thoughts from the heart, contemplate the Path, restrain the body, be careful with speech, and keep the mind under control.
Abandoning anger in one’s practice, patience is the strongest;
abandoning anger and leaving behind pride, one avoids all encounters with craving.
Not becoming attached to name-and-form, one brings about the cessation of suffering through the unconditioned; rising up, one resolves anger and restrains the arising of lust.
By abandoning ignorance and being steadfast, one attains peace in all these respects; by severing anger, one sleeps in peace, and by extinguishing malice, lust, and sorrow.
Anger is the root of poison; the brahmin of gentle mind speaks well and gains renown, for the severance [of defilements] brings freedom from affliction.
Associating with fellow practitioners, one commits evil deeds in detail; later, harboring resentment toward others, one is consumed by the self-tormenting fire of one's own actions.
Lacking shame and remorse, possessing no precepts but only anger, one is dragged away by that anger and finds no weariness in worldly affairs.
The powerful should approach the strong with caution; the powerless should approach the weak with gentleness. Patience is supreme; one should always practice patience toward the weak.
Even if the multitude holds one in contempt, the powerful should exercise patience; patience is supreme; one should always practice patience toward the weak.
Regarding oneself and others, there are three great fears; as one knows what the other does, so should one eliminate it within oneself.
When both follow this principle, I act as a teacher for them: as one knows what the other does, so should one eliminate it within oneself.
The wise overcome the foolish through suffering; those who speak harshly and with evil intent, if they wish to be ever victorious, should remain silent in speech.
For one who commits evil, anger meets with the retribution of anger; by not returning anger for anger, one triumphs over the victor in battle.

Chapter 26: On Defilements (*Rajas*) The Chapter on Defilements, the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Dharmapada*, consists of nineteen verses. Regarding this "Chapter on Defilements," one should distinguish between the pure and the turbid; in training, one ought to remain stainless and refrain from acts of defilement and disgrace.
Born without virtuous conduct, one falls into evil realms at death; dwelling in the Avīci hell, one arrives there with no provisions.
One should seek wisdom to kindle the stability of the mind; by removing defilements and not being stained, one may leave behind the body of suffering.
The wise person proceeds gradually, advancing with steady composure; they wash away the defilements of the mind as a smith refines gold.
When evil arises in the mind, it destroys its own form, just as rust produced by iron consumes the iron itself.
Not reciting is the stain of speech; lack of diligence is the stain of the household;
lack of adornment is the stain of physical form; heedlessness is the stain of one's affairs;
stinginess is the stain of generosity; and unwholesomeness is the stain of conduct.
In this world and in the world beyond, unwholesome dharmas are a constant stain.
Among all stains, none is more severe than delusion. One who trains should abandon evil;
such a bhikṣu is free from stain.
If one lives without shame, like a bird with a long beak, wearing a forced smile while enduring humiliation, this is called a defiled life.
Though integrity and shame may bring hardship, if one seeks purity and upholds righteousness, avoiding disgrace and never acting recklessly, this is called a pure life.
The foolish person delights in killing; their speech lacks sincerity; they take what is not given and lust after the wives of others;
they act according to their whims and violate the precepts, becoming intoxicated by wine.
Such a person, life after life, digs up the very root of their own being.
If a person realizes this, they should not harbor evil thoughts; the fool who associates with what is unrighteous will long burn himself and sink into ruin.
If one practices giving out of a desire for fame or to assemble people through empty pretenses, it is not the entry into pure concentration.
Severing all desires and cutting off the root of the mind’s faculty, guarding single-mindedness day and night, one will surely enter meditative concentration.
Attachment to defilements constitutes dust; following such stained dust leads to outflows. By not being stained and not acting [upon them], one becomes pure and free from delusion.
Seeing that one is being harmed by oneself, one should constantly examine one's inner self; when conduct is tainted by self-deception, it is exhausted and free from defilement.
No fire is hotter than lust; nothing is more swift than anger.
The net of ignorance is most dense; the torrent of craving flows faster than a river.
In empty space there are no tracks; the śramaṇa has no outward thoughts.
All people delight in evil; only the Buddha is pure and free from defilement.
In empty space there are no tracks; the śramaṇa has no external thoughts. All in the world is impermanent; for the Buddha, nothing is "mine. Chapter 27:

On Upholding (Dharmapada, Chapter 27, consisting of seventeen sections). The Chapter on Upholding explains the meaning of the Way. The Dharma prizes virtuous conduct; it does not value greed or extravagance.
One who loves the Way of the Sūtras does not compete for profit; whether there is gain or loss, they remain free from desire and undeluded.
Always compassionate toward those who love learning, they practice with a rectified mind, cherishing and embracing precious wisdom—this is called the Way.
What is called a wise person does not necessarily consist in eloquent speech;
one who is without fear or dread, and maintains goodness, is wise.
One who upholds the Dharma does not do so by means of many words.
Though one may have heard little in the past, if they embody the Dharma in their conduct and guard the Way without forgetting it, they may be said to truly honor the Dharma.
As for what is called "old," it does not necessarily mean advanced age; one whose physical form is mature and hair is white may be merely dull-witted and foolish.
One who upholds the Dharma of Truth, is disciplined, compassionate, and kind, possessing far-reaching clarity and purity—such a person is called an elder.

What is meant by being upright is not having a complexion like a flower; rather, it is one who abandons stinginess, envy, and hollow pretension, whose words and deeds are consistent, who has cast off evil, severed its very roots, and possesses wisdom free from anger.
This is what constitutes true integrity.
What is called a śramaṇa does not necessarily mean one who has shaved his hair; if one speaks falsely, greedily grasps at things, and possesses desires like an ordinary person, he is no such thing.
One who is able to cease evil, who expands and propagates the Way, and who quiets the mind and extinguishes discursive thought—this is a śramaṇa.
One who is called a bhikṣu merely by name is one who begs for food at improper times and engages in sexual misconduct with others.
One who abandons both sin and merit, purely cultivates the holy life, and whose wisdom can destroy evil— this is a true bhikṣu.
What is called benevolent clarity does not mean merely not speaking such words with the mouth; it means that while the mind is not pure and one merely complies outwardly,
if the mind is non-active, internal conduct is pure and empty, and both self and other are extinguished—
this is benevolent clarity.
What is called the Way does not consist in saving a single thing;
it is to provide universal relief to all under heaven, with non-harming as the Way.
To refrain from speaking of the multitude of precepts, yet for my own practice to be full of sincerity—this is the Way.
One who attains concentration must first close and diminish [the senses], seeking peace through mental resolve.
Do not associate with ordinary people; as long as the fetters are not exhausted, one cannot attain liberation.
Chapter 28: On the Path (*Mārga-varga*). This chapter on the path, the twenty-eighth of the *Dharmapada*, explains the essential principles of the way to liberation; it is most sublime.
The Eightfold Path is the supreme way; the Four Truths are the tracks of the Dharma.
Chastity is the most honored of practices; by offering lamps, one will surely obtain eyes.
This path is free from further fear; seeing purity, one then transcends the world.
This can destroy the armies of Māra; through diligent practice, one extinguishes false suffering.
I have already opened the Right Path and manifested great, extraordinary illumination for all.
Having heard this, you should practice it yourselves; through practice, you shall be liberated from the bonds of falsehood.
Birth and death are impermanent and suffering; to be able to perceive them thus is wisdom.
To desire to leave all suffering behind, one practices the Path and removes it all.
Birth and death are impermanent and empty; to be able to perceive them thus is wisdom.
If you wish to leave all suffering behind, you should simply practice the Path with diligence.

When it is time to rise, you should rise immediately; do not be like a fool who hides in a deep abyss, falling into a pit from which there is no escape, calculating and wearying yourself without advancing on the Path.
Mindfulness of what should be remembered is right; mindfulness of what should not be remembered is wrong.
Through wisdom, one does not give rise to the wrong; by contemplating the right path, it is perfected.
Be cautious in speech, guard your thoughts, and do not perform unwholesome deeds with the body.
When these three activities are thus eliminated, the Buddha says one has attained the Path.
If one cuts down a tree but does not cut its root, it will grow back again as long as the root remains.
Only when the root is removed is there no tree; so too, the bhikṣu attains Nirvāṇa.
Unable to sever the tree, relatives cling to one another; bound by greedy thoughts, they are like a calf longing for its mother’s milk.
One who can sever the root of the mind will find that birth and death have no power over them; this is drawing near to the Way and swiftly attaining Nirvana.
Lust leads to old age; hatred leads to illness; delusion leads to death. By eliminating these three, one attains the Way.
Explaining what precedes and understanding what follows, one is liberated from the middle and crosses over to the other shore. When all thoughts are extinguished, there is no more aging or death.
People busy themselves with wives and children, yet do not contemplate the law of illness; when the end of life suddenly arrives, it is like a rushing torrent.
Father and son cannot save one another—what hope can there be for other kin?
When life ends, one relies on kin, like a blind man clutching a lamp.
Understanding this meaning through wisdom, one should cultivate the sutras and precepts; by diligently practicing to transcend the world, all suffering is eliminated.
Far removed from all abysses, like the wind dispersing clouds, having extinguished discursive thought—this is knowledge and vision.
Wisdom is the preeminent leader of the world; delighting in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one understands the true teaching and brings an end to birth and death.
To know that all conditioned phenomena are empty is the vision of wisdom; one becomes weary of and detaches from the suffering of the world, removing it through this path.
To know that all conditioned phenomena are suffering is the vision of wisdom; one becomes weary of and detaches from the suffering of the world, removing it through this path.
That all conditioned phenomena are not the self is the vision of wisdom; one becomes weary of and detests worldly suffering, which is eliminated by following this path.
I speak the Dharma to you: the arrow of craving is what strikes; you should exhort yourself accordingly and receive the words of the Tathāgata.
I have brought the aggregates to extinction; coming and going in birth and death are exhausted.
It is not through a single state of mind that liberation is attained; what is expounded here is the Eye of the Path.
As swift currents pour into the sea, so do the tributary waters flow rapidly until it is full.
Therefore, for the sake of the wise, it is said: one may proceed to partake of the nectar of immortality.
This Wheel of Dharma, never heard before, has been turned out of compassion for sentient beings;
thus, those who serve it pay homage and cross over the three realms of existence.
Three thoughts are to be cultivated as wholesome; three are likewise difficult to master as unwholesome.
From thought arises volitional formation; its cessation constitutes right abandonment.
Through the three concentrations, one turns away from thought; relinquishing attachment, one practices the immeasurables.
Having attained the three and cleared the three caves, one may contemplate the untying of knots.
Knowing that evil is removed by the prohibitions of the precepts, one contemplates the joy of wisdom;
having already understood the rise and fall of the world, one quiets the mind and attains universal liberation.

Chapter 29: On Expansion (*Vipula-varga*). This twenty-ninth chapter of the *Dharmapada*, consisting of fourteen sections, is titled "On Expansion" because it states that all good and evil, though beginning as small, lead to greatness; it serves as a testimony to the meaning of the verses.
Though the gift of peace may be small, its retribution is exceedingly great;
by following wisdom through minor acts of giving, one receives vast blessings.
To labor for others while hoping for their protection, yet having calamity and fault return to oneself, is to encounter widespread resentment.
Having already engaged in many matters, one further creates what is not a matter; through music and negligence, evil habits increase daily.
Practice only with diligence, abandoning what is wrong and cultivating what is right; to cultivate the body and awaken oneself—this is called correct cultivation.
Having personally attained wisdom and being extensively learned, one gradually advances toward universal breadth, like clarified butter cast into water;
whereas lacking the intent for wisdom and disliking learning, one remains congealed and narrow, like curd-butter cast into water.
When one draws near to the Path, its name becomes manifest, like snow upon a high mountain; when one is far from the Path, it is obscure and dark, like an arrow shot in the night.
As a disciple of the Buddha, always remain awake and self-awakened; day and night recollect the Buddha, contemplate the Dharma, and reflect upon the Saṅgha.
As a disciple of the Buddha, one should awaken and realize for oneself; at the close of day, one should contemplate meditation and joyfully delight in single-mindedness.
A person should maintain mindfulness and, with each meal, know moderation;
thus, painful desires will thin out, digestion will be regulated, and longevity will be preserved.
Learning is difficult; renouncing evil is difficult; living as a householder is also difficult;
meeting together and sharing the same benefit is difficult. Among all these difficulties, none surpasses existence.
For a bhikṣu, begging for alms is difficult; how can one not exert oneself?
Through diligence one attains spontaneity, and thereafter has no further desire for human things.
When there is faith, the precepts are perfected;
from the precepts one brings forth much treasure, and through them one also finds harmony and union, receiving offerings wherever one goes.
Sitting alone and lying down in one place, practicing a single path without indulgence, guarding the one to rectify the body—the mind finds joy dwelling among the trees. (30) Chapter Thirty:

The Hell Chapter (*Niraya-varga*), the thirtieth chapter of the *Dharmapada*, consisting of sixteen sections. Regarding the Hell Chapter: it describes the affairs of the hells (*niraya*); having committed evil, one receives evil; drawn by the weight of transgression, one cannot be released.
The hell of lying is near; having done it, one says, "I did not.
One shall suffer both sins in the future, for such conduct drags one away by itself.
Though the Dharma robes are upon his body, he does not restrain himself from evil.
Those who persist in evil conduct will ultimately fall into hell.
To receive offerings without observing the precepts—how could this not be self-destructive?
In death, one must swallow glowing iron balls, burning more fiercely than charcoal embers.
There are four matters of heedlessness:
taking pleasure in violating the wives of others, lying in perilous places which bring no merit, slandering the Three Jewels, and indulging in lewdness as the fourth.
Through such lack of merit one falls into evil states; thus one should fear evil and fear the scarcity of true joy.
When the king’s law imposes heavy punishment, one dies and enters hell.
It is like pulling a blade of grass: if you grasp it too loosely, you will wound your hand;
if one studies the precepts without self-restraint, one becomes a thief to oneself when recorded in the prison registers.
If a person acts with arrogance and indolence, unable to eliminate manifold afflictions,
their holy life will be marred by flaws, and they shall ultimately not receive great merit.
One should constantly perform what ought to be done, maintaining oneself with necessary strength.
Stay far away from all non-Buddhists; do not associate with them as if they were defilements.
By doing what should not be done, one subsequently brings about distress and poison.
Practice goodness and you will always be auspicious and compliant; wherever you go, there will be no regret or stinginess.
Regarding those various evil deeds, whether one intends to commit them or has already done so, this suffering cannot be undone;
the transgression is close at hand and difficult to avoid.
To bear false witness for the sake of ruin, to act with inherent dishonesty, and to slander the virtuous—these bring misery.
He governs the scholars with injustice;
he binds these men in crime, casting them into pits as if fortifying a border city, making it secure both within and without.
Guarding one's own mind, unwholesome states do not arise; yet a deficiency in conduct leads to sorrow and causes one to fall into hell.
To feel no shame where shame is due, and to feel shame where there is no shame, results in false views in this life and a fall into hell after death.
Not fearing what is fearsome, yet fearing what is not fearsome; trusting and inclining toward false views, one falls into hell at death.
Not avoiding what should be avoided, nor approaching what should be approached; habitually practicing false views, one falls into hell at death.
One should approach what is to be approached and distance oneself from what is to be distanced; always maintaining right view.
Upon death, one falls into a good destination.

Chapter 31: The Elephant Simile. This chapter from the *Dharmapada*, the thirty-first, consisting of eighteen verses, titled "The Elephant Simile," teaches people to rectify their own bodies; by performing good, one obtains good, and the retribution of merit is joyful.
Like an elephant in battle, I am not afraid of being struck by arrows; with constant sincerity and faith, I deliver those who lack precepts.
Just as an elephant that is well-trained may be used as a royal mount, one who is disciplined becomes a noble person and thus receives sincerity and faith.
Though it be well-trained, like a newly broken-in steed, even the most excellent elephant is not equal to one who has trained himself.
That [other] cannot reach where people do not go; only he who has trained himself can reach the destination of training.
Like the elephant named Dhanapāla, fierce and difficult to restrain,
who remains violent and unruly even when bound and denied food—
so too those submerged in evil conduct are constantly fettered by their own greed.
That elephant knows no satiety; therefore, it repeatedly enters the womb.
When one’s fundamental intent is pure conduct, and one dwells constantly in what is peaceful, one completely abandons and subdues the fetters, just as a hook restrains and tames an elephant.
Delighting in the Path and being heedless not, one can always guard the mind;
this is what uproots bodily suffering, like an elephant emerging from a pit.
If one finds a worthy and capable companion, they shall walk together with vigor in practicing the good.
One who can subdue all that is heard and reaches the goal without losing the intended meaning;
one who, failing to find a virtuous companion, walks alone rather than practicing with a wicked and fierce one;
and who would rather go alone than commit evil—such a person cuts off the king’s dominion and its villages. It is better to be alone than to do evil.
It is better to walk alone in goodness than to be a companion to the foolish;
to walk alone without committing evil, like an elephant guarding itself when startled.
To be born with benefit and peace is good; to have companions who are gentle and harmonious is peace.
To have one's life end in peace through merit is bliss; to refrain from committing any evil is bliss.
To have a mother in one’s family is joy; to have a father is likewise joy.
That there are śramaṇas in the world is joy; that the Way prevails throughout the world is joy.
One who maintains the precepts finds peace until old age; faith is what rectifies that which is crooked and leads to goodness.
Wisdom is the supreme peace for the body, and refraining from evil is the greatest peace.
Like a well-trained horse that goes wherever it is directed, so too are those with faith, virtue, and diligence.
The essential requirements for meditative concentration are:
the establishment of clear knowledge and conduct, patience, gentleness, and mental stability; these sever all suffering and allow one to proceed according to one's will.
From this one proceeds to meditative concentration, like a horse well-tamed; by severing ill-will and becoming free from outflows, one experiences celestial bliss.
Without indulging in self-indulgence, one remains ever awake; compared to a feeble horse, such a person is superior, having abandoned evil and become virtuous.

Chapter 32: On Lust (*Kāma-vagga*). This chapter on lust from the *Dhammapada*, the thirty-second, consists of thirty-two sections. Regarding this chapter on lust: one should despise sexual desire and worldly affection, for it is because of these that calamities arise in abundance among the people of the world.
With the mind fixed on sexual conduct, the branches of craving increase;
spreading and flourishing intensely, the monkey of greed leaps about for its fruit.
Enduring suffering for the sake of love, one becomes attached to the world through craving.
Sorrow and affliction grow day and night, spreading like creeping vines.
Humans are deluded by affection and unable to abandon their passions;
thus, their sorrows and attachments increase, filling the pond with a constant murmur.
The reasons for sorrow and grief—the sufferings of the world are not one—are simply due to the existence of craving; when craving is abandoned, there is no sorrow.
When one’s own mind is at peace, sorrow is cast aside; if there is no craving, how can there be a world?
Without sorrow, without defilement, and without seeking, how could one find peace through attachment?
When there is sorrow at the time of death, one brings many relatives along;
traversing the long road of grief, one constantly falls into peril through the suffering of attachment.
One who practices the Way does not associate with desire; first uprooting the source of craving so that it has no place to take root—do not be like one cutting reeds, allowing the mind to grow again.
Just as when a tree’s roots are deep and firm, it grows back even if cut down;
so too, if the mind of craving is not completely eradicated, one will inevitably undergo suffering once again.
Like a monkey that has escaped from a tree yet, having found release, runs back toward the tree once more.
So it is with all people: having emerged from prison, they enter it again.
Greed is their constant flow; habituated to arrogance, their thoughts dwell upon sensual desire. Shrouded by this, they see nothing at all.
The stream of all mental activity flows forth; the fetter of craving is like a creeping vine.
Only through the discerning vision of wisdom can one sever the root-source of the mind.
For it is moistened by craving and grows its spreading tendrils through discursive thought.
Craving is deep and bottomless; through it, old age and death increase.
The branches of rebirth do not cease; one merely feeds upon greed and desire, nourishing enmity and swelling the graveyards, while the fool remains ever in a state of frantic haste.
Though a prison may have hooks and iron plates, the wise do not call it secure;
the fool sees his wife and children and becomes deeply attached through craving, which is truly secure.
The wise declare that craving is a prison, deep and firm, from which it is difficult to escape.
Therefore, one should sever and cast it away; by not regarding desire, one can find peace.
When seeing forms, the mind becomes deluded; failing to contemplate impermanence, the fool deems them beautiful and good—how could he know they are not real?
Enveloped by the pleasures of lust, they are like silkworms making cocoons;
the wise are able to sever and cast them away, not looking back as they eliminate all suffering.
Those whose minds dwell on negligence perceive lust as pure.
When the sentiment of affection increases intensely, from this one constructs the prison of suffering.
One who awakens the mind to extinguish lust constantly contemplates the impurity of desire;
from this one escapes the evil prison and is able to sever the affliction of old age and death.
Shrouded by the net of desire, covered by the canopy of craving,
and bound in prison by self-indulgence, one is like a fish entering the mouth of a trap,
waiting to be seized by old age and death, like a calf seeking its mother’s milk.
Having abandoned desire and extinguished the traces of craving, having emerged from the net with nothing further to obscure him,
having exhausted the path and removed the bonds of the prison, liberated from both this world and the next,
and having already attained the practice that transcends all limits— he is a man of great wisdom.
Do not associate with those who distance themselves from the Dharma, nor become stained by attachment;
for one who does not sever the three times will again fall into extreme conduct.
If one awakens to all phenomena, one can remain unattached to them.
The liberation from all craving—this is the penetration of the noble mind.
Among all gifts, the gift of the Dharma is supreme; among all flavors, the flavor of the Dharma is supreme;
among all joys, the joy of the Dharma is supreme; and the exhaustion of craving surpasses all suffering.
The fool binds himself with greed and does not seek to cross to the other shore;
because greed is the site of ruin, it harms others and harms oneself as well.
With the mind of craving and desire as the field, lust, anger, and delusion serve as the seeds.
Therefore, those who practice the perfection of giving transcend the world and attain immeasurable merit.
When a merchant has few companions but much merchandise, he is filled with trepidation and fear;
since the thieves of sensual desire harm one's life, the wise do not crave such desires.
If the mind finds pleasure, it constitutes desire; why need it be limited to the five desires alone?
To sever the five desires by renouncing what is pleasurable—this is to be a true hero.
Without desire, there is no fear; in tranquil serenity, there is no sorrow or affliction.
Desiring to eliminate the fetters and knots, one thereby emerges forever from the abyss.
If you wish to know my origin, it arises from mental volition (*saṃskāra*).
If I do not direct volition toward you, then you shall no longer exist.
When felling a tree, one must suddenly cease; if the tree produces various evils and the tree is cut down with its roots remaining, the bhikṣu will not attain parinirvāṇa.
Indeed, if one does not fell the tree, even if there are few or many remaining kinsmen, the mind remains bound to them, like a calf seeking its mother.

Chapter 33: On Gains and Offerings (*Lābha-saṃyutta*). This chapter of the *Dharmapada*, consisting of twenty verses, is titled "On Gains and Offerings. It exhorts one to restrain oneself and guard against greed; by contemplating the virtues [of others], one should not give rise to defilement.
The plantain perishes because of its fruit; the same is true for bamboo and reeds.
The kyang-horse dies from pregnancy; the man ruins himself through greed.
Thus, greed brings no benefit; one should know that it arises from delusion.
The fool brings harm to the worthy, and his head and neck are parted from the earth.
Heaven rains down the seven treasures, yet desire remains insatiable; pleasure is slight while suffering is great—only the awakened one is truly worthy.
Though they possess celestial desires, through wisdom they renounce them and are free from greed; delighting in detachment from affection, they become disciples of the Buddha.
Those who distance themselves from the Path and follow what is deviant, monks who covet sustenance, harbor stinginess in their hearts, providing only for their own kin.
Do not rely on this sustenance; though you may abandon transgressions for the sake of your family, this is not the ultimate intention—what benefit is there in such worldly pursuits?
To act foolishly according to foolish schemes only increases desire and pride; how strange that such failure results in a state far removed from Nirvana!
One who knows this truly is a bhikṣu, a son of the Buddha; not delighting in gain and offerings, he dwells in seclusion with his mind withdrawn.
Attaining [realization] himself, he does not rely on it; not looking for expectations from others, he observes that other bhikṣus have not yet reached right concentration.
Now, one who wishes to settle the destiny of life should quiet the mind and reflect within; they should not be preoccupied with calculating the number of their garments or food and drink.
One who wishes to settle the destiny of life should quiet the mind and reflect within; they should attain contentment and maintain the practice of a single dharma.
One who wishes to settle the destiny of life should quiet the mind and reflect within, like a mouse hiding in its burrow.

Practicing the teachings in seclusion, one should restrain both benefit and hearing; by upholding the precepts and reflecting upon them, one will be praised for wisdom; remain pure and auspicious, and do not be indolent.
Though possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge and being liberated from outflows, they have little wisdom and scant discernment, and lack any mindfulness.
Regarding food and drink, they receive benefit from others, yet harbor evil dharmas and envy those who provide offerings.
Having formed many enmities and attachments, though forcibly donning the dharma robes, they look only for food and drink and do not follow the Buddha’s teaching.
One should know this to be a fault; to nourish such a life is a great fear. To take little is to have no sorrow; thus the bhikṣu releases his mind.
If one does not eat, life cannot be sustained; who then could refrain from considering food?
Since establishing food as the priority is fundamental, knowing this, one should not be envious.
Envy first wounds oneself and only then wounds others; when one strikes another, one receives a strike in return.
This cannot be remedied;
it would be better to chew burning stones and swallow molten copper than, lacking the precepts, to consume the faithful offerings of others.

34. Chapter on the Śramaṇa (Śramaṇavarga). This thirty-fourth chapter of the Dharmapada, the Chapter on the Śramaṇa, consists of thirty-two verses. As for this "Chapter on the Śramaṇa," it instructs through the rectitude of the Dharma; when disciples receive and practice it, they attain the Way, achieve liberation, and become pure.
With eyes, ears, nose, and mouth restrained, and body and mind always maintaining rectitude—
the bhikṣu who practices in this way can escape from all suffering.
Do not recklessly offend with hands or feet; be moderate in speech and act in accordance with what you do.
Always find joy within in meditative concentration, guarding the single practice of stillness.
In study, one must guard the mouth; let words be measured and composed, and take the meaning of the Dharma as your stability.
One's speech must be gentle;
one should delight in the Dharma and desire the Dharma, contemplating and abiding in the Dharma. A bhikṣu who relies upon the Dharma is upright and not wasteful.
One who trains should not seek profit, nor should they be attached to the conduct of others; if a bhikṣu delights in others, he will not attain concentration of mind.
A bhikṣu who takes little, thereby attaining freedom from accumulation, is praised by gods and men, and is born pure and free from defilement.
A bhikṣu practices loving-kindness, cherishing and honoring the Buddha’s teachings; deeply entering into śamatha and vipaśyanā, he attains peace by extinguishing conditioned formations.
Regarding all name-and-form as non-existent and free from delusion, neither approaching nor grieving, such a one is truly a bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu rows the boat; when it is empty within, it is light. To eliminate lust, anger, and delusion—this is nirvāṇa.
Abandoning the five, severing the five, contemplating the five faculties, and being able to discern the five—one then crosses the river’s abyss.
Practice meditation without negligence; do not be disturbed by sensual desires. Do not swallow molten copper and scorch your own body with self-inflicted pain.
Without meditation there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no meditation. The Path proceeds from meditation and wisdom, leading to the attainment of Nirvana.
One should train in entering emptiness, dwelling in stillness to settle the mind; delighting in solitude and seclusion, contemplate the Dharma with a single-minded focus.
Constantly restrain the five aggregates and subdue the mind like water; pure and harmoniously joyful, one partakes of the flavor of ambrosia.
Not grasping at anything, he is a wise bhikṣu; guarding his senses and contented, he maintains the precepts in their entirety.
In life he should practice purity, seeking virtuous teachers and friends; through wisdom one becomes a true person, crossing over suffering to reach joy.
Like the flowers of the *vairaṇyaka* tree, which fall of their own accord when ripe, one who abandons lust, anger, and delusion finds the cycle of birth and death naturally resolved.
Stilling the body and stilling speech, with the mind maintained in profound silence— the bhikṣu who thus renounces the world attains this state of quiescence.
One should command oneself, contending within with the mind; guarding the body and mindful of the Truths, a bhikṣu finds peace.
Regarding myself as myself, yet reckoning that there is no self, one should thus diminish the "self"; through such discipline, one becomes a sage.
Delighting in the Buddha’s teaching, one may find abundant joy; reaching the state of profound stillness, through the cessation of formations, one attains eternal peace.
If one practices even slightly in accordance with the Buddha’s precepts, this will illuminate the world like the sun free from clouds.
Abandoning pride without remainder and free from arrogance, like a lotus born from the water,
one who trains in renouncing both this world and the next knows that such a state is superior to the former.
Severing attachment without lingering longing, one remains untainted like a lotus.
The bhikṣu crosses the river; he excels because he understands desire.
Having severed the stream, he relies on himself; with a mind that has departed, he repels desire. If the benevolent one does not cut off desire, his single-mindedness still wanders.
Do it! Do it! You must exert yourself in self-restraint; yet if you abandon the household life and become lax, your mind will still be defiled once more.
For one whose practice is lax, how can the wearying mind be eliminated?
Without pure brahmacarya, how can the Great Treasure be attained?
What is the conduct of a śramaṇa?
If one does not restrain the mind as desired, it clings at every step and follows wherever thoughts run.
Though the *kāṣāya* robe is draped over the shoulders, it does nothing to diminish one's evil; those who practice evil and pursue evil shall fall into the evil realms.
One who is undisciplined is difficult to admonish, like a withered tree in the wind; if you act for your own sake, why do you not exert yourself?

True "stilling of the mind" is not merely shaving the head; one who is arrogant and lacks precepts cannot still the mind. Only by abandoning greed and contemplating the Way does one truly accord with the stilling of the mind.
One who has stilled the mind, though not shaven, who is free from negligence and possesses faith, and is able to extinguish all suffering—such a one is a supreme *śramaṇa*.

Chapter 35: The Brahmin (*Brāhmaṇavarga*). This chapter consists of forty verses. Regarding the "Brahmin Chapter," one whose conduct is pure and whose learning is untainted may be called a practitioner of the Way (*mārga-carin*).
One who has crossed over by cutting off the stream, who is free from desire like Brahmā, and who knows that all formations have been exhausted—
such a one is called a brahmin. One who, by means of the non-dual dharma, crosses the abyss with purity and whose fetters of desire are all untied— such a one is called a brahmin.
When there is no "this" in that, and "that" is already empty of itself; when one has abandoned sensual lust, he is called a brahmin.
When one contemplates the stainless, acts without leakage, and does not give rise to further seeking, he is called a brahmin.
The sun shines by day, the moon shines by night; armor and weapons illuminate the army, and meditation illuminates the practitioner;
when a Buddha appears in the world, he illuminates all darkness.
One is not a śramaṇa by shaving the head, nor is one a brāhmaṇa by claiming auspiciousness;
he who is able to abandon all evils is a seeker of the Way (mārgajina).
One who has emerged from evil is a brāhmaṇa; one who has entered the right path is a śramaṇa.
Abandoning all my defiled conduct is what constitutes leaving the home life.
If one relies on [the truth] yet the mind has no attachments— having already relinquished and corrected [all faults]—
this is the extinction of all suffering.
One whose body, speech, and mind are pure and without fault, who is able to relinquish the three modes of action—such a person is called a brahmin.
If one’s mind clearly understands the Dharma taught by the Buddha, and observes the mind as its own refuge, then purity is like water.
One does not become a brahmin by binding one's hair in a topknot;
it is through practicing the Dharma with sincerity and maintaining purity that one is truly noble.
If there is no wisdom, what is the use of adorning the hair? What purpose is served by clothing made of grass?
If one is not free from attachment within, what benefit is there in renouncing externals?
One who wears tattered and coarse robes, personally upholds the practice of the Dharma, and dwells in seclusion in contemplation—such a person is called a *brahmin*.
The Buddha does not teach him to praise himself or boast; if he is truthful and not false, [he is a true brahmin].
One who is thus is a brahmin;
one who has severed all desires and whose will is not lustful, having cast off the category of desire—such a one is called a brahmin;
one who has cut the river of birth and death, who is able to endure and cross over, and who has awakened for himself and emerged from the moat—such a one is called a brahmin.
When reviled or struck, one receives it silently without anger; possessing the power of patience, such a one is called a brahmin.
If one is treated with malice or deceit, one simply remains mindful of guarding the precepts, rectifying the body and self-disciplining; such a one is called a brahmin.
One who has cast off evil states from the mind, like a snake shedding its skin, and is not defiled by sensual desires— he is called a brahmin.
One who realizes that birth is suffering and, from this realization, extinguishes the will [for rebirth], and is able to lay down the heavy burden— he is called a brahmin.
One who understands subtle wisdom, distinguishes the path from what is not the path, and embodies the practice of the supreme meaning—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
One who has abandoned the household life and is free from the fear of home, possessing few desires and little seeking—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
One who has renounced the livelihood of living beings, harbors no intent to harm, and causes no affliction or distress—[such a one is called a *brahmin*].
This is called a brahmin:
one who avoids strife and does not contend, who is not resentful when wronged, and who responds with kindness to those who come with malice—this is called a brahmin;
one who has cast off lust, anger, and delusion, along with pride and all evils, like a snake shedding its skin—this is called a brahmin.
One who has severed worldly affairs, whose mouth utters no coarse words, and who discerns the Eightfold Path with certainty—
such a one is called a brahmin.
Regarding all evil dharmas of the world, whether long or short, great or small, he neither grasps nor rejects them— such a one is called a brahmin.
One who is pure in conduct in this life and free from defilement in the next, who neither clings nor abandons— such a one is called a brahmin.
One who has cast off the body and is without dependence, who does not recite heterodox practices, and who walks toward the nectar of cessation—
such a one is called a brahmin.
One who has forever eliminated both paths of sin and merit, who is free from sorrow and free from dust—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
One whose mind is joyful and stainless like the full moon, who has already removed all slander and defamation—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
Seeing the deluded come and go, falling into the moat and suffering there, he desires to cross alone to the other shore.
One who does not rely on the words of others, but solely brings about cessation and non-arising—
such a one is called a brahmin. One who has severed affectionate ties, left the home life free from desire, and whose craving for existence is exhausted—
such a one is called a brahmin.
Detached from human gatherings, not falling into the assembly of devas, returning to no assembly—such a one is called a brahmin.
Having abandoned pleasure and being without pleasure, with extinction and no feverish heat, the steadfast one who has transcended all worlds—such a one is called a brahmin.
One for whom birth has already ended, who goes nowhere upon death, awakened in peace and without dependence.
This is called a brahmin;
having crossed over the five realms of existence, one knows not where one shall fall; with habitual tendencies exhausted without remainder, this is called a brahmin;
before, after, and in the middle, there is nothing at all; without grasping and without relinquishing, this is called a brahmin.
Most heroic and most courageous, able to liberate oneself and cross over, with awakened mind unmoving—this is called a brahmin;
having attained the essential, birth is exhausted; with wisdom reaching the profound Way, as clear-sighted as one who can remain silent.
This is what is called a *brahmin*.

Chapter 36: Nirvāṇa. The Chapter on Nirvāṇa, the thirty-sixth chapter of the *Dharmapada*, describes the great destination of the Way: tranquility, extinction, and the crossing over from the fear of birth and death.
Patience is the supreme self-guarding; Nirvana is what the Buddha calls the highest.
To leave home and not violate the precepts, to quiet the mind and do no harm—this is the greatest benefit of being free from illness, the greatest wealth of contentment, and the best of friends.
Nirvāṇa is the supreme joy;
hunger is the greatest illness, and conditioned existence is the greatest suffering. Having understood this with certainty, Nirvāṇa is the highest bliss.
Few travel upon the path of goodness, while many head toward the evil realms; having understood this with certainty, Nirvāṇa is the ultimate peace.
From causes one arises in goodness; from causes one falls into evil; through causes one attains nirvāṇa—the objects of perception are likewise so.
Deer rely on the wilds; birds rely on the void; dharmas return to their retribution; the True Persons return to extinction.
Is the beginning not like non-existence?
The beginning is not like non-existence; this is called non-attainment, and there is also no thought.
The mind is difficult to see, but its habitual tendencies can be observed; it is only by awakening to desire that one fully perceives.
The absence of delight is the end of suffering; dwelling in craving and desire is the increase of pain.
When wisdom is not clear, one cannot master purity; by not approaching anything, one reaches the end of suffering.
Seeing there is seeing, hearing there is hearing, thinking there is thinking, and cognizing there is cognizing;
yet beholding without attachment and without cognition, relinquishing all—this is the attainment of the limit.
Eliminating the perception of the body, extinguishing painful formations, and with consciousness already exhausted, suffering comes to an end.
When there is reliance, there is movement; when there is emptiness, there is purity. Movement is not near, nor is there pleasure;
when pleasure is not near, one attains tranquility. Being tranquil and already tranquil, one has transcended coming and going.
Coming and going cease, and there is no birth-and-death; birth-and-death being severed, there is neither "this" nor "that";
"this" and "that" being severed, both are extinguished; when extinction is without remainder, suffering is eliminated.
A bhikṣu who has birth in the world, Who has existence and performs conditioned activities,
Will have no birth and no existence, And will perform no actions and engage in nothing.
Only he who is free from conceptualization Is able to attain self-mastery.
There is no birth and no further existence; there is no action and no sphere of activity.
Those who conceive of birth, existence, action, and activity have not attained the essential point.
If one has already understood non-arising, there is neither existence nor the performance of action.
Thus there arises that which possesses the essential point; from that which possesses birth it has already arisen.
Through the performance of formations one brings about death and birth, acting as the opening and the fruit of the Dharma.
From the causal condition of nutriment existence comes to be; from nutriment one encounters sorrow and joy.
As for this essential cessation, there are no further traces of mental formations.
All phenomena of suffering have been exhausted; with the cessation of formations, one rests in profound stillness.
O Bhikṣu, I have already known this: there are no longer any realms of sensory entry.
There is no entrance into space, nor any use of the sense-bases as entrances;
there is no entrance of thought or non-thought. There is neither this world nor the world beyond, nor any perception of sun or moon; there is no going forth, nor anything to which one is attached.
I have no more coming and going; neither departing nor arriving, neither passing away nor being reborn—this limit is Nirvana.
Such as this, both with form and without form, suffering and pleasure are thereby liberated.
What is seen is no longer feared; speechless, yet speaking, one is free from doubt.
Having severed the arrow of existence, one encounters folly without any dependence.
This is the foremost bliss; this path is tranquil and unsurpassed.
When receiving insult, let the mind be like the earth; practice patience as one would a door-sill.
Pure like water, free from defilement, when birth is exhausted, there is no further experience of such things.
Victories and triumphs are not to be relied upon; even victory remains but suffering.
One should seek for oneself the state of transcendence; having transcended, there is nothing further to arise.
By exhausting the old, one does not create the new; weary of the womb, one ceases sexual conduct.
When the seeds are scorched, they do not sprout again; when the mind is exhausted, it is extinguished like a fire.
The womb is a sea of filth; why indulge in lustful conduct?
Though there may be superior realms above, none equal Nirvāṇa.
Fully knowing that all [defilements] are severed, one no longer clings to the world.
Having abandoned all as if entering parinirvāṇa, this is the most excellent among all paths.
The Buddha has manifested the Dharma of Truth; with wisdom and courage, one can uphold it.
When conduct is pure and free from blemish, one knows for oneself that one has crossed over to peace in the world.
In the pursuit of the Way, first distance yourself from desire; Early on, don the precepts of the Buddha’s teaching.
To extinguish evil to its ultimate limit Is as easy as a bird soaring through the void.
If you have already understood these verses of Dharma, Then embody the practice of the Way with a sincere heart.
This is crossing to the far shore of birth and death, where suffering ends and there is no affliction.
The Dharma has neither kin nor stranger; it does not distinguish between the weak and the strong.
The essential point lies in the absence of conceptualization; when the fetters are untied, one attains purity.
The person of superior wisdom is satiated with this decaying body; it is precarious, fragile, and not truly real.
Suffering abounds while joy is scarce, and among its nine orifices, not one is pure.
With wisdom, he exchanges the precarious for the secure, casting off attachment to escape all hardships.
When the body decays and dissolves into froth, wisdom perceives it and abandons all craving.
Contemplating the body as a vessel of suffering—subject to birth, old age, and sickness—one casts off defilements and practices purity; thus one may attain great peace.
Relying on wisdom to dispel the false, one does not accept outflows and attains their exhaustion;
through pure conduct, one reaches transcendence, and there are no devas or humans who do not pay homage. 37.

Chapter on Birth and Death (Saṃsāra-varga), the thirty-seventh chapter of the *Dharmapada*, consisting of eighteen sections. Regarding this "Chapter on Birth and Death," it speaks of the human soul: when the physical body perishes, the spirit remains, transmigrating according to its past actions.
Life is like fruit waiting to ripen; one always fears it will fall and rot.
All that is born possesses suffering; who can attain immortality?
From the beginning, one has delighted in sensual affection, entering into lust as if into bubbles and shadows.
Receiving a physical form, life is like a flash of lightning; day and night it flows on, difficult to stop.
This body is a thing destined for death, while the spirit is a formless phenomenon.
Even if one dies and is born again, one’s transgressions and blessings do not perish.
From beginning to end, it spans more than a single lifetime;
following from ignorance and craving for a long duration, one undergoes suffering and pleasure from this point on. When the body dies, the spirit does not perish.
The four great elements constitute "form," while consciousness and the four aggregates are called "name."
Its mental states are of eighteen kinds, and its objects of perception arise from twelve.
The abodes of the spirit are ninefold; birth and death continue without cessation.
The worldly fools do not hear this, for they are shrouded in darkness and lack the divine eye.
Self-anointed with the three impurities, blind and with deluded views,
they claim that death is like life, or else they claim that death is total annihilation.
Consciousness creates the three realms and the five destinies of good and evil.
Moving in secret and arriving silently, where one goes is like an echo responding.
Whether in the realm of desire, form, or formlessness, everything is due to past actions;
just as a seed follows its original form, the natural retribution accords with the intention.
The spirit takes the body as its name, just as fire follows the form of its characters:
when applied to a candle, it is "candle-fire," and it follows charcoal, grass, dung, or firewood.
When mental phenomena arise, they arise; when phenomena cease, they cease.
Rise and fall are like rain and hail; turning and turning, one does not recognize oneself.
The conscious spirit wanders through the five realms, with no place where it does not undergo change.
Casting off a body and receiving another again is like a wheel revolving upon the ground.
Just as a person leaves their old dwelling to occupy a new body, the spirit takes the physical form as its abode; though the form perishes, the spirit does not perish.
The spirit residing within the physical frame is like a sparrow hidden inside a casket.
When the vessel breaks, the sparrow flies away; when the body perishes, the spirit departs and is reborn.
Those of deluded nature harbor notions of purity and permanence, notions of a pleasant self, and notions of doubt.
Such resentment and longing are not the supreme path; the Buddha says these are called ignorance.
One root and two successions, three stains and five expanses;
the thirteen matters of the various seas, the abyssal dissolution and transcendence bring joy.
When these three matters are severed, one knows the body has no value.
Vitality, breath, warmth, and consciousness—when these abandon the body, it passes away.
When one lies dead upon the ground, they are like grass, devoid of all sensation.
Observing their condition thus, one sees that they are but illusions, born of folly and greed.

Chapter 38: The Benefits of the Path (*Mārga-hita-varga*). The thirty-ninth chapter of the *Dharmapada*, titled "The Benefits of the Path," concerns the conduct of rulers, fathers, and teachers, who reveal the virtuous path and lead others toward rectitude.
People know how to honor their superiors: the sovereign, father, teacher, and the Way-master;
through faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, they find ultimate auspiciousness and peace in their rebirths.
Possessing the blessings of merit from past lives, they are born as honored ones in this world.
He pacifies the world through the Way; those who revere the Dharma follow him without exception.
As the sovereign and leader of ministers and subjects, he always treats those below with compassion and love.
He leads by means of the Dharma and precepts, demonstrating to them what is auspicious and what is calamitous.
Abiding in security, one does not forget danger; with clear deliberation, blessings increase in thickness.
Such is the reciprocal retribution of merit and virtue—it makes no distinction between the noble and the lowly.
He who acts as a general of the world maintains rectitude and does not bend to injustice.
One whose mind is disciplined overcomes all evils; such a person is a Dharma King.
Seeing correctly, they are able to bestow kindness; being benevolent and loving, they delight in benefiting others.
Having benefited them with impartiality, the multitude thus becomes attached and affectionate toward them.
Just as when a bull crosses a ford, if the leader goes straight, those following him also go straight;
so too, when one upholds the Dharma with an undistorted mind, the entire multitude attains universal peace.
Do not recklessly disturb the divine elephant, lest you invite the calamity of suffering.
If one kills oneself out of malice, one will ultimately never reach the realm of goodness.
The virtue of precepts is something to rely upon; the retribution of merit constantly follows one.
Seeing the Dharma as the guide for humanity, one will ultimately remain far removed from the three evil realms.
Vigilance in the precepts removes suffering and fear; such merit is honored throughout the three realms.
Ghosts, nāgas, and malevolent poisons cannot harm one who upholds the precepts.
Those who are unrighteous and lack sincerity, who are deceitful, false, and fond of strife—[they cannot harm the precept-keeper].
One should know to distance oneself from those who associate with fools and give rise to much demerit;
one should know to draw near to the virtuous and noble, whose speech is truthful and sincere, who are learned,
and who are complete in ethical conduct— for by associating with the wise, truthfulness and goodness increase.
One who speaks well but does not observe the precepts, whose will is distracted and lacks virtuous conduct—even if they dwell in seclusion—this is not the study of the Dharma.
To speak beautifully is the highest; to speak according to the Dharma is second.
1. To speak with affection, to speak what is pleasing to others—these three; to speak with sincerity and not to deceive—this is the fourth. 2.
Without cause, one gains a sharp blade that, by its very nature, strikes one’s own body.
3. The ignorant student delights in false speech; their conduct drags them toward misfortune and ruin.
Lust, anger, and delusion—these three are not the roots of goodness;
by them the body brings harm to itself, and retribution arises from delusion and craving.
Those with merit become devas or humans; through unrighteousness, one receives an evil form.
The Sage’s clear and solitary vision always skillfully upholds the Buddha’s command.
The virtue of the precepts is karma for future lives; by performing merit, it follows the person.
Devas and humans praise the virtuous; with a rectified mind, there is no lack of peace.
If one commits evil and does not think of stopping, binding oneself day after day without remorse, life will pass away like the flow of a river; fearing this, one should guard the precepts.
Now that my head and upper body have been overtaken by white hair, and since the divine messengers have already summoned me, this is precisely the time for me to renounce the household life.

Chapter 39: On Auspiciousness (*Maṅgala-vagga*) The Chapter on Auspiciousness, the thirty-ninth of the *Dhammapada*, consists of nineteen verses. It concerns the method of cultivating oneself—abandoning evil and embracing good—which ultimately brings forth profound and lasting blessings.
The Buddha, the Honored One, surpasses all devas; the Tathāgata constantly manifests the true meaning.
When a brahmin ascetic came to ask, "What is auspicious?
the Buddha, out of compassion, spoke for him the essential points of true reality.
To have faith and delight in the True Dharma is the supreme auspiciousness;
not to follow gods or humans, nor to seek luck through chance,
nor to offer prayers and sacrifices to deities— this is the supreme auspiciousness.
Associate with the wise and choose to dwell with the virtuous; always prioritize the cultivation of merit and virtue.
Discipline yourself to follow what is true and correct—this is the supreme auspiciousness.
Abandon evil and turn toward the good; avoid alcohol and know how to exercise self-restraint.
To be free from lust for women’s beauty is the greatest auspiciousness;
to possess great learning and act according to the precepts, to study the Dharma and Vinaya with diligence,
and to cultivate oneself without contention— this is the greatest auspiciousness.
To dwell in filial piety and serve one's parents, to manage the household and provide for wife and children,
and not to engage in empty practices— this is the most auspicious thing.
To be neither arrogant nor conceited, to know contentment, and to reflect upon the cycle of cause and effect.
To recite and study the sutras at the proper times is the most auspicious thing;
To always practice patience regarding what one hears, to delight in seeing śramaṇas,
and to listen and receive the teachings whenever they are expounded— this is the most auspicious thing.
Observing the fast and practicing the pure life, always desiring to see the noble and holy ones,
and relying upon those of wisdom— this is the most auspicious thing.
Possessing faith in virtue and morality, with a right intention free from doubt, one attains the highest blessing.
To seek liberation from the three evil realms is the most auspicious;
to practice generosity with an impartial mind, to honor those who have attained the Way,
and to revere all devas and humans— this is the most auspicious.
Always desiring to leave behind greed, delusion, and anger,
and being able to practice the vision of the path of truth— this is the most auspicious.
If one abandons what is not one's duty and is able to diligently apply oneself to the practice of the path, [this is the most auspicious].
Constantly attending to what ought to be done is the most auspicious;
acting for the sake of all under heaven, establishing a mind of great compassion,
practicing benevolence to bring peace to sentient beings— this is the most auspicious.
Those who seek auspicious fortune should have faith and reverence for the Buddha;
those who seek auspicious fortune should hear the meaning of the Dharma verses;
those who seek auspicious fortune should make offerings to the Saṅgha.
To possess the purity of ethical discipline is the most auspicious;
when the wise dwell in the world, they constantly practice auspicious conduct,
thereby personally attaining the vision of wisdom— this is the most auspicious.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the brahmin was filled with great joy in his heart;
he immediately came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
